      "text": " / math.log(2.0) / SCORED_BYTES\n\n\ndef parity():\n    p = os.path.join(RES, \"parity.txt\")\n    if not os.path.exists(p):\n        return None\n    txt = io.open(p, encoding=\"utf-8\").read()\n    out = {}\n    for m in re.finditer(r\"== parity (\\w+) ==\\s*NATS_TOTAL ([0-9.eE+-]+)\", txt):\n        out[m.group(1)] = m.group(2)          # kept as TEXT: G2 asks for bit-identity\n    return out\n\n\ndef load(path):\n    \"\"\"Group every measurement by (shape, bench, attn, attnr), apply G0, then take the median of\n    the survivors.  Run 2 is rep-major, so a key carries three separate single-rep records; run 1\n    was arm-major and carries one record per key.  Both load; only the first can survive G0 when\n    the machine misbehaves, which is the point of the change.\"\"\"\n    raw = {}\n    for r in json.load(open(path, encoding=\"utf-8\")):\n        shape = r[\"label\"].split(\"_\")[0]\n        o = r[\"median_rep_organs_ms\"]\n        key = (shape, r[\"bench\"], r.get(\"attn\", \"serial\"), r.get(\"attnr\", \"none\"))\n        raw.setdefault(key, []).append(\n            dict(organs=o, tok_s=r[\"median_tok_s\"], iqr=r[\"iqr_tok_s\"],\n                 W=sum(o[k] for k in WEIGHT_ORGANS), attn_ms=o[\"attention\"],\n                 f=sum(o[k] for k in FIXED)))\n    # G0 is a CELL-level test: the minimum W of the whole cell is the uncontended reference.\n    cells = {}\n    for (shape, b, at, ar), v in raw.items():\n        cells.setdefault((shape, b), []).extend(v)\n    floor = {k: min(x[\"W\"] for x in v) for k, v in cells.items()}\n    A, G0 = {}, {}\n    for (shape, b, at, ar), v in sorted(raw.items()):\n        w0 = floor[(shape, b)]\n        keep = [x for x in v if x[\"W\"] <= w0 * (1.0 + G0_TOL)]\n        G0.setdefault((shape, b), []).append((at, ar, len(v), len(keep),\n                                              max(x[\"W\"] for x in v) / w0 - 1.0))\n        if len(keep) < min(G0_MIN_SURVIVORS, len(v)):\n            continue                      # arm has no clean measurement; cell will be voided\n        D, F, L, NH, NKV, HD, V = SHAPES[shape]\n        pos = (b + 1) / 2.0\n        med = lambda f: sorted(f(x) for x in keep)[len(keep) // 2]\n        A[(shape, b, at, ar)] = dict(\n            shape=shape, bench=b, attn=at, attnr=ar, n=len(v), n_kept=len(keep),\n            tok_s=med(lambda x: x[\"tok_s\"]), iqr=med(lambda x: x[\"iqr\"]),\n            attn_ms=med(lambda x: x[\"attn_ms\"]), f=med(lambda x: x[\"f\"]),\n            W=med(lambda x: x[\"W\"]), pos=pos, L=L, NH=NH, NKV=NKV, HD=HD,\n            expf_calls=L * NH * pos, v_unique=L * NKV * HD * pos * 4.0,\n            v_touched=L * NH * HD * pos * 4.0)\n    return A, G0\n\n\ndef report_g0(G0):\n    print(\"## G0 -- the weight path is invariant across arms; anything else is the machine \"\n          \"(brief s8.3)\\n\")\n    print(\"| cell | measurements | kept | discarded | worst `W` excess | verdict |\")\n    print(\"|---|---|---|---|---|---|\")\n    dead = set()\n    for (shape, b), rows in sorted(G0.items()):\n        n = sum(r[2] for r in rows)\n        k = sum(r[3] for r in rows)\n        worst = max(r[4] for r in rows)\n        starved = [r for r in rows if r[3] < min(G0_MIN_SURVIVORS, r[2])]\n        ok = not starved\n        if not ok:\n            dead.add((shape, b))\n        print(\"| %s @%d | %d | %d | %d | +%.1f%% | %s |\"\n              % (shape, b, n, k, n - k, 100.0 * worst,\n                 \"PASS\" if ok else \"**VOID -- %d arm(s) with no clean measurement: %s**\"\n                 % (len(starved), \", \".join(r[1] for r in starved))))\n    print()\n    return dead\n\n\ndef cell(A, shape, b):\n    \"\"\"The decomposition at one (shape, context), or None if the sweep is missing an arm.\"\"\"\n    g = lambda at, ar: A.get((shape, b, at, ar))\n    s1, s2, a0 = g(\"serial\", \"none\"), g(\"serial2\", \"none\"), g(\"avx4\", \"none\")\n    if not (s1 and s2 and a0):\n        return None\n    c = dict(shape=shape, bench=b, base=a0, serial=s1, serial2=s2)\n    c[\"X_serial\"] = s2[\"attn_ms\"] - s1[\"attn_ms\"]\n    c[\"R\"] = s1[\"attn_ms\"] - c[\"X_serial\"]\n    c[\"X_avx4\"] = a0[\"attn_ms\"] - c[\"R\"]\n    for name, two, three in ((\"S\", \"sm2\", \"sm3\"), (\"Y\", \"av2\", \"av3\")):\n        t2, t3 = g(\"avx4\", two), g(\"avx4\", three)\n   ",

      "text": "l the\nyoung men of our university, who allows you to dwell in his house, who\nentrusts you with all the thoughts of his heart, by what offense has\nhe deserved, that you should thus mean-spiritedly deny him?\"\n\n\"If I were to answer now,\" returned Antonio angrily, \"that you do not\nknow him, that I have reasons, and the fullest, to think otherwise of\nhim, again you would not understand me.\"\n\n\"Verily,\" said Alfonso with a sneer, \"you have already scaled so high\ninto the most secret places of his philosophy, that the common\nunfavoured child of earth is unable to follow you. Here again one sees\nthat half-merit and quarter-merit puff themselves up the most. Pietro\nAbano is more lowly-minded than you, his feeble mimic.\"\n\n\"You are unmannerly!\" exclaimed the young Florentine irritated to the\nutmost. \"If I were now to assure you by my honour, by my faith, by\nheaven, and by everything which must needs be holy and venerable to\nyou and me, that in all Italy, in all Europe, there is no such wicked\nvillain, no so atrocious hypocrite as this....\"\n\n\"Who?\" shouted Alfonso.\n\n\"Pietro Abano,\" said Antonio now grown calm: \"what would you say\nthen?\"\n\n\"Nothing!\" furiously cried the other, who had not allowed him to\nfinish: \"save that you, and everybody else who dares to speak in that\nway, are the paltriest knaves that ever had the audacity to blaspheme\nholy things. Draw, if you would not be called a mean coward as well as\na base slanderer.\"\n\nAntonio's drawn sword met the challenger with the same speed; and it\nwas in vain that a hoarse anxious voice cried out to them: \"Hold!\"\nAlfonso was wounded in the breast; and the blood at the same time ran\nfrom Antonio's arm.\n\nThe old priest, who had wisht to separate the quarrellers, now\nhastened forward; bound up their wounds and stancht the blood; then he\ncalled to some students that he had seen a little way off, and told\nthem to carry the wounded Alfonso to the city.\n\nBefore he was removed, Antonio went up to him and whispered in his\near: \"If you are a man of honour, not a word about the cause of our\nfray will pass over your lips. In four days time we will meet again:\nand if you are not of my way of thinking then, I am ready to give you\nany satisfaction.\"\n\nAlfonso pledged his solemn promise; all the bystanders too assured\nAntonio that the wound as well as the whole affair should be kept a\nsecret, not to expose him to any danger.\n\nWhen they were all gone Antonio walkt with the priest Theodore deeper\ninto the wood.\n\n\"Why,\" began the latter, \"will you, for a fiend's sake, make over your\nown soul to hell? I see, you are now of a different opinion; but is\nthe sword the spokesman that should preach truth to a brother?\"\n\nAntonio felt in doubt how much he should disclose to the monk; however\nhe said nothing about the wonderful event that had befallen him, and\nonly entreated that, at the approaching festival of Easter, he might\nbe allowed to enter the great church during high mass through the\nsacristy, near the altar.\n\nAfter some objections Theodore complied, though he could not conceive\nwhat was the youth's purpose in asking for this permission. All\nAntonio said further was: \"I wish to bring a friend into the church\nthat way, whose entrance at the great door might perhaps be stopt.\"\n\n       *       *       *       *       *\n\nAll the bells in the city were ringing, that the holy feast of Easter\nmight be kept with gladness and devotion. The people flockt toward the\ndome, to celebrate the most joyous of Christian festivals, and also to\nbehold the renowned Apone in his new dignity. The students escorted\ntheir illustrious teacher, who walkt along amid the reverent\nsalutations of the nobles, the council, and the citizens, in seeming\npiety and humility, an example to all, the pride of the city, the\ninspiring model of the youth. At the door of the cathedral the crowd\nshrank back in timid respect, to make way for their honoured bishop,\nwho, in the garb of a prelate, with the golden chain round his neck,\nwith his white beard and the white locks on his head, might be\ncompared to an emperor or an ancient doctor of the church",

tell to me?\n    At such a butt, sir, he said,\n      As men use in my country.\n\n    William went into a field,\n      And with him his two brethren:\n    There they set up two hazel rods\n      Twenty score paces between.\n\n    I hold him an archer, said Cloudesly,\n      That yonder wand cleaveth in two.\n    Here is none such, said the king,\n      Nor none that can so do.\n\n    I shall assay, sir, said Cloudesly,\n      Or that I farther go.\n    Cloudesly with a bearyng[72] arrow\n      Clave the wand in two.\n\n    Thou art the best archer, then said the king,\n      For sooth that ever I see.\n    And yet for your love, said William,\n      I will do more mastery.\n\n    I have a son is seven year old,\n      He is to me full dear;\n    I will him tie to a stake;\n      All shall see, that be here;\n\n    And lay an apple upon his head,\n      And go six score pace him fro',\n    And I myself with a broad arrow\n      Shall cleave the apple in two.\n\n    Now haste thee, then said the king,\n      By Him that died on a tree,\n    But if thou do not as thou hast said,\n      Hanged shalt thou be.\n\n    An thou touch his head or gown,\n      In sight that men may  In the earth he drove a stake:\n\n    And bound thereto his eldest son,\n      And bade him stand still thereat;\n    And turned the child's face him from,\n      Because he should not start.\n\n You must tell me!\xe2\x80\x9d\n\nHe was silent.\n\n\xe2\x80\x9cI don\xe2\x80\x99t understand your why, Count,\xe2\x80\x9d she continued, \xe2\x80\x9cbut it\xe2\x80\x99s hard for\nme... I confess it. For some reason you wish to deprive me of our former\nfriendship. And that hurts me.\xe2\x80\x9d There were tears in her eyes and in her\nvoice. \xe2\x80\x9cI have had so little happiness in life that every loss is hard\nfor me to bear.... Excuse me, good-by!\xe2\x80\x9d and suddenly she began to cry\nand was hurrying from the room.\n\n\xe2\x80\x9cPrincess, for God\xe2\x80\x99s sake!\xe2\x80\x9d he exclaimed, trying to stop her.\n\xe2\x80\x9cPrincess!\xe2\x80\x9d\n\nShe turned round. For a few seconds they gazed silently into one\nanother\xe2\x80\x99s eyes\xe2\x80\x94and what had seemed impossible and remote suddenly became\npossible, inevitable, and very near.\n\n\n\n\n\nCHAPTER VII\n\nIn the winter of 1813 Nicholas married Princess Mary and moved to Bald\nHills with his wife, his mother, and S\xc3\xb3nya.\n\nWithin four years he had paid off all his remaining debts without\nselling any of his wife\xe2\x80\x99s property, and having received a small\ninheritance on the death of a cousin he paid his debt to Pierre as well.\n\nIn another three years, by 1820, he had so managed his affairs that he\nwas able to buy a small estate adjoining Bald Hills and was negotiating\nto buy back Otr\xc3\xa1dnoe\xe2\x80\x94that being his pet dream.\n\nHaving started farming from necessity, he soon grew so devoted to it\nthat it became his favorite and almost his sole occupation. Nicholas was\na plain farmer: he did not like innovations, especially the English ones\nthen coming into vogue. He laughed at theoretical treatises on estate\nmanagement, disliked factories, the raising of expensive products,\nand the buying of expensive seed corn, and did not make a hobby of any\nparticular part of the work on his estate. He always had before his\nmind\xe2\x80\x99s eye the estate as a whole and not any particular part of it. The\nchief thing in his eyes was not the nitrogen in the soil, nor the oxygen\nin the air, nor manures, nor special plows, but that most important\nagent by which nitrogen, oxygen, manure, and plow were made\neffective\xe2\x80\x94the peasant laborer. When Nicholas first began farming\nand began to understand its different branches, it was the serf who\nespecially attracted his attention. The peasant seemed to him not merely\na tool, but also a judge of farming and an end in himself. At first\nhe watched the serfs, trying to understand their aims and what they\nconsidered good and bad, and only pretended to direct them and give\norders while in reality learning from them their methods, their manner\nof speech, and their judgment of what was good and bad. Only when he\nhad understood the peasants\xe2\x80\x99 tastes and aspirations, had learned to talk\ntheir language, to grasp the hidden meaning of their words, and felt\nakin to them did he begin boldly to manage his serfs, that is, to\nperform toward them the duties demanded of him. And Nicholas\xe2\x80\x99 management\nproduced very brilliant results.\n\nGuided by some gift of insight, on taking up the management of the\nestates he at once unerringly appointed as bailiff, village elder, and\ndelegate, the very men the serfs would themselves have chosen had they\nhad the right to choose, and these posts never changed hands. Before\nanalyzing the properties of manure, before entering into the debit and\ncredit (as he ironically called it), he found out how many cattle the\npeasants had and increased the number by all possible means. He kept the\npeasant families together in the largest groups possible, not allowing\nthe family groups to divide into separate households. He was hard alike\non the lazy, the depraved, and the weak, and tried to get them expelled\nfrom the commune.\n\nHe was as careful of the sowing and reaping of the peasants\xe2\x80\x99 hay\nand corn as of his own, and few landowners had their crops sown\nand harvested so early and so well, or got so good a return, as did\nNicholas.\n\nHe disliked having anything to do with the domestic serfs\xe2\x80\x94the \xe2\x80\x9cdrones\xe2\x80\x9d\nas he called them\xe2\x80\x94and everyone said he spoiled them by his laxity.       "text": " some\ndreadful thing were suddenly to happen; if a house were just about to\nfall on one;--don't you know how one would long to sit down and shut\none's eyes and wait, and wait? Well, when this terrible feeling came\nover him, the priest quickly pressed the cross to his lips, without a\nword--a little silver cross it was--and he kept on pressing it to the\nman's lips every second. And whenever the cross touched his lips, the\neyes would open for a moment, and the legs moved once, and he kissed the\ncross greedily, hurriedly--just as though he were anxious to catch hold\nof something in case of its being useful to him afterwards, though he\ncould hardly have had any connected religious thoughts at the time. And\nso up to the very block.\n\n\"How strange that criminals seldom swoon at such a moment! On\nthe contrary, the brain is especially active, and works\nincessantly--probably hard, hard, hard--like an engine at full pressure.\nI imagine that various thoughts must beat loud and fast through\nhis head--all unfinished ones, and strange, funny thoughts, very\nlikely!--like this, for instance: 'That man is looking at me, and he\nhas a wart on his forehead! and the executioner has burst one of his\nbuttons, and the lowest one is all rusty!' And meanwhile he notices and\nremembers everything. There is one point that cannot be forgotten, round\nwhich everything else dances and turns about; and because of this\npoint he cannot faint, and this lasts until the very final quarter of\na second, when the wretched neck is on the block and the victim listens\nand waits and _knows_--that's the point, he _knows_ that he is just _now_\nabout to die, and listens for the rasp of the iron over his head. If I\nlay there, I should certainly listen for that grating sound, and hear\nit, too! There would probably be but the tenth part of an instant left\nto hear it in, but one would certainly hear it. And imagine, some people\ndeclare that when the head flies off it is _conscious_ of having flown\noff! Just imagine what a thing to realize! Fancy if consciousness were\nto last for even five seconds!\n\n\"Draw the scaffold so that only the top step of the ladder comes in\nclearly. The criminal must be just stepping on to it, his face as white\nas note-paper. The priest is holding the cross to his blue lips, and the\ncriminal kisses it, and knows and sees and understands everything.\nThe cross and the head--there's your picture; the priest and the\nexecutioner, with his two assistants, and a few heads and eyes below.\nThose might come in as subordinate accessories--a sort of mist. Don't deny the\nfact, for you did, of course. Besides, you stop philosophizing when you\nare telling about anything.\"\n\n\"Why are you ashamed of your stories the moment after you have told\nthem?\" asked Aglaya, suddenly.\n\n\"How silly you are!\" said Mrs. Epanchin, looking indignantly towards the\nlast speaker.\n\n\"Yes, that wasn't a clever remark,\" said Alexandra.\n\n\"Don't listen to her, prince,\" said Mrs. Epanchin; \"she says that sort\nof thing out of mischief. Don't think anything of their nonsense, it\nmeans nothing. They love to chaff, but they like you.       "text": "stinction lost. Compare also the\nuse of _fa_, as a common auxiliary; nor are these exceptions, but, on\nthe contrary, characteristic examples. Also to enunciate the language\nrightly one must hold the back and neck erect and the muscles firm.\n\nIn some languages the speaker thinks of himself and his completed action\nas inseparable, as a single idea, as the Latin _edi_ for I have eaten;\nin others he thinks of himself subconsciously as possessing the results\nof his action, as our _I have eaten_; and in others, as among the Irish\npeasantry, he separates himself and his action entirely, as _I am after\neating_. In some grammars, as in Maya, the verbal concept starts with\nthe past; in others, as our own, we live in the present; in the Welsh,\nthe future is the chief tense. The mere choice of _shall_ or _will_ as\nthe first person future auxiliary denotes a specific mental quality.\n\nNow the expression of all these infinite shades of relationtionship[TN-5]\nbetween the self, the activity and the world, is achieved in two ways:\nposition or placement--syntax; and form. The customary division of\nlanguages is into Monosyllabic, Agglutinative, Incorporating, and\nInflectional, and this division will suit our purpose, though it must be\nused with care. It is held in the ordinary theory that these classes must\nrepresent successive stages of linguistic perfection, each in turn being\nhigher in the scale than the other, they having grown one from the other\nas the race advanced. By the theory the monosyllabic is lower than the\nagglutinative, and inherently less useful. But the theory does not work\nout in practical application to the facts we have to deal with, for while\nwe cannot find still left in the world any agglutinative languages\nrepresentative of sufficient culture to bring into our present\nconsideration, we do find a monosyllabic in the highest rank, and meeting\nthe highest cultural requirements. In short, the latter may be\ntheoretically the inferior tool, but the genius of thought behind is\ngreater than the form. One man can draw a masterpiece with a burnt stick,\nanother only paint a daub with all the brushes made. Once again we must\nnot judge by our preconceived preferences of form.\n\nOmitting therefore the modern remnants of agglutinating languages,\noutside of America, as affording us no literary material of value for\nour study, we shall find at once drawn across all the other great\nclasses a single broad line of division, between the ideographic and the\nliteral--the same as already mentioned. And the moment we draw this line\nas an exponent of the mental and spiritual thought-life of the different\npeoples, we shall find it not only molding their language forms, both\nwritten and spoken, but manifest as well in their art, philosophy, and\neven their social polity. And of course we must be fair in our\ncomparisons, and not set a Chinese coolie in the concrete against an\nEnglish statesman, nor any concrete example of another kind of culture\nin its decay with the highest bloom to which we believe our own type to\nbe able to carry us.\n\nIt would be absurd to say that the ratiocinative, literal mind is higher\nthan the ideal. One man sees directly the meaning of the things, the\nevents and situations before him; another reasons it all out. And\ncontrary to many of our current beliefs, the former is often the man of\naction; he sees at a flash to the heart of the matter, and gets things\ndone. His thought, his activity, is vivid; and his words are likely to\nbe so as well. The idealist, if he be broadminded, and not merely\nsentimental, is indeed likely to be the practical man. And the type of\nmind that is made manifest to us by these great non-Aryan languages and\ntheir forms, is the former. Of course idealism in its decadence becomes\nnegative, inactive, self-consuming and no longer creative.       "text": "ow came up and\nhopped around, as if waiting for the man to move, and so to see if he\nwere really dead. After awhile, the crow, to make quite sure, perched\non a branch above the man's head and dropped a piece of twig on to his\nface! It was at this stage that the man decided to be alive, and, taking\nup his gun, shot the crow.\n\nThere may be some exaggeration in the bushmen's tales of the crow's\ncunning, but there is quite enough of ascertained fact to show that the\nbird is as devilish in its ingenuity as in its cruelty. In most parts of\nAustralia there is a reward paid for every dead crow brought into the\npolice offices. Still, in spite of constant warfare, the bird holds its\nown, and very rarely indeed is its nest discovered--a signal proof of\nits precautions against the enmity of man.\n\nTo turn to a more pleasant type of feathered animal. On the whole, the\nmost distinctly Australian bird is the kookaburra, or \"laughing\njackass.\" (A picture of two kookaburras faces page 1 of this volume.\nThey were drawn for me by a very clever Australian black-and-white\nartist, Mr. Norman Lindsay.) The kookaburra is about the size of an owl,\nof a mottled grey colour. Its sly, mocking eye prepares you for its\nnote, which is like a laugh, partly sardonic, partly rollicking. The\nkookaburra seems to find much grim fun in this world, and is always\ndisturbing the Bush quiet with its curious \"laughter.\" So near in sound\nto a harsh human laugh is the kookaburra's call that there is no\ndifficulty in persuading new chums that the bird is deliberately mocking\nthem. The kookaburra has the reputation of killing snakes; it certainly\nis destructive to small vermin, so its life is held sacred in the Bush.\nAnd very well our kookaburra knows the fact. As he sits on a fence and\nwatches you go past with a gun, he will now and again break out into his\ndiscordant \"laugh\" right in your face.\n\nThe Australian magpie, a black-and-white bird of the crow family, is\nalso \"protected,\" as it feeds mainly on grubs and insects, which are\nnuisances to the farmer. The magpie has a very clear, well-sustained\nnote, and to hear a group of them singing together in the early morning\nsuggests a fine choir of boys' voices. They will tell you in Australia\nthat the young magpie is taught by its parents to \"sing in tune\" in\nthese bird choirs, and is knocked off the fence at choir practice if it\nmakes a mistake. You may believe this if you wish to. I don't. But it\ncertainly is a fact that a group of magpies will sing together very\nsweetly and harmoniously.\n\nOne could not exhaust the list of Australian birds in even a big book.\nBut a few more call for mention. There is the emu, like an ostrich, but\nwith coarse wiry hair. The emu does damage on the sheep-runs by breaking\ndown the wire fences. (Some say the emu likes fencing wire as an article\nof diet; but that is an exaggeration founded on the fact that, like all\ngreat birds, it can and does eat nails, pebbles, and other hard\nsubstances, which lodge in its gizzard and help it to digest its food.)\nOn account of its mischievous habit of breaking fences the emu is\nhunted down, and is now fast dwindling. In Tasmania it is altogether\nextinct. Another danger to its existence is that it lays a very handsome\negg of a dark green colour. These eggs are sought out for ornaments, and\nthe emu's nest, built in the grass of the plain (for the emu cannot fly\nnor climb trees), is robbed wherever found.\n\nThe brush turkey of Australia is strange in that it does not take its\nfamily duties at all seriously.       "text": " study in a weary school.\n     O for the folly of the child!\n      The ready courage of the fool!\n     Lord, crush our knowledge utterly\n      And make us humble, simple men;\n     And cleansed of wisdom, let us see\n      Our Lady Folly's face again.\n\n\n\n\nMadness\n\n     (For Sara Teasdale)\n\n\n\n     The lonely farm, the crowded street,\n      The palace and the slum,\n     Give welcome to my silent feet\n      As, bearing gifts, I come.\n\n     Last night a beggar crouched alone,\n      A ragged helpless thing;\n     I set him on a moonbeam throne --\n      Today he is a king.\n\n     Last night a king in orb and crown\n      Held court with splendid cheer;\n     Today he tears his purple gown\n      And moans and shrieks in fear.\n\n     Not iron bars, nor flashing spears,\n      Not land, nor sky, nor sea,\n     Nor love's artillery of tears\n      Can keep mine own from me.\n\n     Serene, unchanging, ever fair,\n      I smile with secret mirth\n     And in a net of mine own hair\n      I swing the captive earth.\n\n\n\n\nPoets\n\n\n\n     Vain is the chiming of forgotten bells\n      That the wind sways above a ruined shrine.\n     Vainer his voice in whom no longer dwells\n      Hunger that craves immortal Bread and Wine.\n\n     Light songs we breathe that perish with our breath\n      Out of our lips that have not kissed the rod.\n     They shall not live who have not tasted death.\n      They only sing who are struck dumb by God.\n\n\n\n\nCitizen of the World\n\n\n\n     No longer of Him be it said\n     \"He hath no place to lay His head.\"\n\n     In every land a constant lamp\n     Flames by His small and mighty camp.\n\n     There is no strange and distant place\n     That is not gladdened by His face.\n\n     And every nation kneels to hail\n     The Splendour shining through Its veil.\n\n     Cloistered beside the shouting street,\n     Silent, He calls me to His feet.\n\n     Imprisoned for His love of me\n     He makes my spirit greatly free.\n\n     And through my lips that uttered sin\n     The King of Glory enters in.\n\n\n\n\nTo a Blackbird and His Mate Who Died in the Spring\n\n     (For Kenton)\n\n\n\n     An iron hand has stilled the throats\n      That throbbed with loud and rhythmic glee\n     And dammed the flood of silver notes\n      That drenched the world in melody.\n     The blosmy apple boughs are yearning\n     For their wild choristers' returning,\n      But no swift wings flash through the tree.\n\n     Ye that were glad and fleet and strong,\n      Shall Silence take you in her net?\n     And shall Death quell that radiant song\n      Whose echo thrills the meadow yet?\n     Burst the frail web about you clinging\n     And charm Death's cruel heart with singing\n      Till with strange tears his eyes are wet.\n\n     The scented morning of the year\n      Is old and stale now ye are gone.\n     No friendly songs the children hear\n      Among the bushes on the lawn.\n     When babies wander out a-Maying\n     Will ye, their bards, afar be straying?\n      Unhymned by you, what is the dawn?\n\n     Nay, since ye loved ye cannot die.\n      Above the stars is set your nest.\n     Through Heaven's fields ye sing and fly\n      And in the trees of Heaven rest.\n     And little children in their dreaming\n     Shall see your soft black plumage gleaming\n      And smile, by your clear music blest.\n\n\n\n\nThe Fourth Shepherd\n\n     (For Thomas Walsh)\n\n\n\n       I\n\n\n     On nights like this the huddled sheep\n      Are like white clouds upon the grass,\n     And merry herdsmen guard their sleep\n      And chat and watch the big stars pass.\n\n     It is a pleasant thing to lie\n      Upon the meadow on the hill\n     With kindly fellowship near by\n      Of sheep and men of gentle will.\n\n     I lean upon my broken crook\n      And dream of sheep and grass and men --\n     O shameful eyes that cannot look\n      On any honest thing again!\n\n     On bloody feet I clambered down\n      And fled the wages of my sin,\n     I am the leavings of the town,\n      And meanly serve its meanest inn.\n\n     I tramp the courtyard stones in grief,\n The\nkernel does `_mm256_shuffle_epi8(tbl, idx)` with `idx` = the loaded code bytes (`engine.c:115, 125,\n134`). **CONFIRM: 9 states carry 4 bits of information and occupy 8 bits solely because `pshufb`\naddresses byte lanes.** The 16-entry LUT with 7 dead slots is the fingerprint of that choice.\n\n### Q4.2 The cost, quantified \xe2\x80\x94 and it lands on the wrong side\n\nThe clean nibble layout packs **two `t` indices per byte** (not two `m`), so the two halves feed two\ndifferent LUT tables into the *same* accumulator and no lane reordering is needed anywhere in the hot\nloop. Per 32-byte load:\n\n| | current | nibble-packed |\n|---|---|---|\n| codes per 32 B load | 32 (64 weights) | 64 (128 weights) |\n| `vmovdqu` codes | 1 | 1 |\n| unpack (`vpand`, `vpsrlw`, `vpand`) | 0 | **3** |\n| LUT broadcast (`vmovdqu` + `vpbroadcasti128`) | 1 | 2 |\n| `vpshufb` | 1 | 2 |\n| `acc_add_i8x32` (1 `vextracti128` + 2 `vpsrldq` + 4 `vpmovsxbd` + 4 `vpaddd`) | 11 | 22 |\n| **total ops per 64 codes** | **30** (= 2 \xc3\x97 15) | **33** |\n\n**+10 % compute for \xe2\x88\x9250 % bytes.** On a bandwidth-bound path that is a ~1.8\xc3\x97 win. On a **compute-bound**\npath it is a ~10 % **loss**.\n\n**Q3.2 established that this path is compute-bound.** The dense LUT-MLP is fully L3-resident (2.25 MiB)\nwith zero gather and still runs at 11.40 GB/s where the same silicon does 185 GB/s on resident fp32\nGEMV. Even the DRAM-streamed bench tops out at 17.0 GB/s against a 40\xe2\x80\x9344 GB/s aggregate ceiling \xe2\x80\x94\n**2.4\xc3\x97 of bandwidth headroom the kernel cannot consume.** Halving code bytes does not make the kernel\nfaster, because its throughput is denominated in *weights per second*, not bytes per second, and\nnibble-packing adds operations per weight.\n\n### Q4.3 Verdict: **(b) real but not free \xe2\x80\x94 and its value is on the footprint axis, not the speed axis**\n\n- **Streamed bytes: genuinely halved.** 0.5 \xe2\x86\x92 0.25 B/weight. CONFIRM.\n- **Time: approximately unchanged, plausibly ~10 % worse** on the measured evidence that the LUT path\n  is compute-bound. **REFUTE the word \"free.\"**\n- **Controller-1's derived conclusion is right on footprint and wrong on speed.** On footprint,\n  0.5 \xe2\x86\x92 0.25 is 2\xc3\x97 and 0.5 \xe2\x86\x92 0.2 (trit-pack) is 2.5\xc3\x97, so trit-pack does add only **1.25\xc3\x97** over\n  nibble-packing \xe2\x80\x94 that arithmetic CONFIRMS. But \xc2\xa78.G's framing of trit-pack as \"a 2.4\xe2\x80\x932.5\xc3\x97 reduction\n  in **streamed bytes**\", read as a throughput claim, is what is actually wrong, and Controller-1\n  inherits that framing rather than challenging it.\n- **Where nibble-packing genuinely pays: the SKU table.** It moves S2's second column and Q1's\n  condition (1): at 0.25 B/weight a 64B-param donor fits under 16 GB and a 128B donor under 32 GB. For\n  Q1's 80B/A3B case it takes resident weights from ~41 GB to ~21 GB. That is real, it is large, and it\n  is the reason to build it \xe2\x80\x94 **not** tok/s.\n- **The actual speed lever is elsewhere and is bigger than both packing and dispatch.**\n  `acc_add_i8x32` (`engine.c:106-110`) spends **11 of 15 ops** widening int8 \xe2\x86\x92 int32 on *every*\n  shuffle. Accumulating in int16 with periodic widening (or `vpmaddubsw`-style pairing) attacks the\n  term that actually caps the kernel at 11\xe2\x80\x9317 GB/s. It is bit-exactness-gated work with an existing\n  harness (`--kselftest`, `engine.c:844+`). **Recommend costing that before either packing variant.**\n\n**Measurement required before acting on any of this:** implement nibble unpack behind a flag, run\n`--kselftest` for bit-exactness against `ref_t3`, then `run_expert_rate` at both packings across the\nQ3.3 size sweep. If the nibble rate in *codes/s* falls by \xe2\x89\xa410 % while bytes halve, the packing is a\nfootprint win at negligible speed cost \xe2\x80\x94 which is the outcome I predict.\n\n---\n\n## Q2 \xe2\x80\x94 30B sparse-MoE vs 8B dense: the Principal vs Controller-1\n\n### Q2.1 Which organ goes down which path in `engine.c`\n\nTwo paths exist and the assignment is not a matter of opinion:\n\n- **fp32 GEMV** \xe2\x80\x94 `matvec` / `dotf` (`engine.c:100`): `in_proj`, `x_proj`, `dt_proj`, `out_proj`,\n  `qkv`, `o`, `router_w`,",
